rows.stem:
Study the following cases :

(i) \(\mathrm{CuSO_4 + Mg \longrightarrow}\)

(ii) \(\mathrm{FeSO_4 + Pb \longrightarrow}\)

(iii) \(\mathrm{CaSO_4 + Al \longrightarrow}\)

(iv) \(\mathrm{ZnSO_4 + Ca \longrightarrow}\)

The case/cases in which new product(s) will form is/are :
rows.solution:
A metal displaces another metal from a solution of its salt only if it is more reactive. In the reactivity series, Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > Cu.

(i) Magnesium is more reactive than copper, so it displaces copper:

\(\mathrm{CuSO_4 + Mg \rightarrow MgSO_4 + Cu}\)

(ii) Lead is less reactive than iron, so there is no reaction.

(iii) Aluminium is less reactive than calcium, so there is no reaction.

(iv) Calcium is more reactive than zinc, so it displaces zinc:

\(\mathrm{ZnSO_4 + Ca \rightarrow CaSO_4 + Zn}\)

New products form in (i) and (iv), which is option (C) (i) and (iv).

rows.subtopic: Human Brain and Protection of Nervous Tissue
rows.stem: The part of the hind-brain controlling involuntary actions such as salivation and vomiting in humans is :
rows.solution:
The medulla, in the hind-brain, controls involuntary actions such as blood pressure, salivation and vomiting. (The cerebellum, also in the hind-brain, keeps posture and balance; the cerebrum is the fore-brain.)

This is option (D) Medulla.

rows.stem: Temporary finger-like extensions on the cell surface to take in food is formed in :
rows.solution:
*Amoeba* takes in food using temporary finger-like extensions of its cell surface (pseudopodia). They fuse over the food particle and form a food vacuole, in which the food is digested.

This is option (B) *Amoeba*.

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Solenoid
rows.stem: The strength of the magnetic field produced inside a current carrying long straight solenoid does *not* depend upon :

options.label: A
options.text: Area of cross-section of the tube of the solenoid

options.label: B
options.text: Number of turns per unit length in the solenoid

options.label: C
options.text: Direction of current flowing through the coil of the solenoid

options.label: D
options.text: Material of the core of the solenoid

rows.solution:
Inside a long solenoid the field is uniform. Its strength is \(B = \mu_0 n I\) for an air core: it is set by the number of turns per unit length and the current, and a soft iron core makes it much stronger. So the number of turns and the material of the core both matter.

Reversing the current reverses the direction of the field but leaves its strength unchanged, so the strength does not depend on the direction of the current.

The formula also contains no area: the field inside a long solenoid does not depend on the area of cross-section of the tube. So the choice "Area of cross-section of the tube of the solenoid" is equally correct, and the question as printed has two right answers. The marking scheme keys only the direction of the current and prints no note accepting the other.

The marking scheme's answer is option (C) Direction of current flowing through the coil of the solenoid.

rows.subtopic: Common Salt and Chemicals from It
rows.stem: Giving reason, state the advantage of using baking powder over baking soda for the preparation of bread or cakes.
rows.solution:
Baking soda alone, on heating, gives sodium carbonate:

\(\mathrm{2NaHCO_3 \xrightarrow{\text{heat}} Na_2CO_3 + H_2O + CO_2}\)

The sodium carbonate left in the bread or cake gives it a bitter taste.

Baking powder is baking soda mixed with a mild edible acid such as tartaric acid. When it is heated or mixed with water, the acid reacts with the baking soda and releases carbon dioxide, which makes the bread or cake rise and become soft and spongy:

\(\mathrm{NaHCO_3 + H^+ \rightarrow CO_2 + H_2O}\) + sodium salt of the acid

The acid neutralises the base, so no sodium carbonate is left and there is no bitter taste. That is the advantage of baking powder.

rows.stem: State the main function of arteries. Why do they have thick and elastic walls ?
rows.solution:
Arteries carry oxygenated blood away from the heart to the various organs of the body. (The pulmonary artery is the exception: it carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.)

They have thick, elastic walls because blood leaves the heart under high pressure. The thick elastic walls withstand this pressure, stretching and recoiling with each heartbeat.

rows.stem:
(a) Explain how the proteins control the ‘characteristics’ in an organism with the help of an example of ‘short height’ trait in pea plant.

(b) Name the information source of making proteins in a cell.
rows.solution:
(a) Plant height depends on the amount of a plant growth hormone. The hormone is made with the help of an enzyme, which is a protein, and the enzyme is made according to the information in a gene (a specific DNA sequence). If the gene gives a less efficient enzyme, less hormone is made, and the plant is short. So the gene controls the trait through the protein it makes.

(b) DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) in the cell is the information source for making proteins.

rows.stem: A voltage source sends a current of 2 A to a resistor of \(40\,\Omega\) connected across it for 5 minutes. Calculate the electrical energy supplied by the source.
rows.solution:
Here \(I = 2\) A, \(R = 40\,\Omega\) and \(t = 5\) min \(= 300\) s.

Electrical energy \(= I^2Rt = (2)^2 \times 40 \times 300 = 48000\) J.

So the source supplies 48000 J (48 kJ).

rows.stem: How is a double displacement reaction different from a displacement reaction ? Explain giving example in the form of balanced chemical equations.
rows.solution:
In a displacement reaction, a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. In a double displacement reaction, two compounds exchange their ions.

Displacement: iron displaces copper from copper sulphate solution; the blue solution turns pale green and copper is deposited.

\(\mathrm{Fe(s) + CuSO_4(aq) \rightarrow FeSO_4(aq) + Cu(s)}\)

Double displacement: sodium sulphate and barium chloride solutions exchange ions, and a white precipitate of barium sulphate forms.

\(\mathrm{Na_2SO_4(aq) + BaCl_2(aq) \rightarrow BaSO_4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}\)

rows.stem:
(a) Enlist any two nitrogenous waste products removed from the blood of human kidney.

(b) Name the capillary cluster formed by the branch of renal artery in the Bowman’s capsule.

(c) Depict in the form of a flow chart the path of the urine formed in each kidney until it is finally passed out through the urethra.
rows.solution:
(a) Urea and uric acid.

(b) The glomerulus.

(c) The urine formed in each kidney passes as follows:

Kidney \(\rightarrow\) Ureter \(\rightarrow\) Urinary bladder \(\rightarrow\) Urethra

It is stored in the urinary bladder until it is passed out through the urethra.

rows.chapter: The Human Eye and the Colourful World
rows.subtopic: Defects of Vision and their Correction
rows.stem: A person has to keep reading material much beyond 25 cm (say at 50 cm) from the eye for comfortable reading. Name the defect of vision he is suffering from. List two causes responsible for arising of this defect. Draw a labelled diagram showing correction of this defect using eye-glasses. Are these glasses convergent or divergent of light ?
rows.solution:
The person cannot see nearby objects clearly, though distant ones are clear, so the defect is hypermetropia (far-sightedness).

Two causes: (i) the focal length of the eye lens is too long; (ii) the eyeball has become too small.

Diagram: draw the eye with a convex lens in front of it. Mark N at 25 cm from the eye and N' at 50 cm, the near point of the defective eye. Rays from an object at N pass through the convex lens and bend so that they appear to come from N' (shown by dotted lines produced back); the eye lens then focuses them on the retina. Label the convex lens, the retina, N and N', and draw arrows on the rays.

The glasses are convex lenses, so they are convergent of light. (Here the lens must form the image at 50 cm of an object at 25 cm: \(\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{50} + \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{1}{50}\), so \(f = +50\) cm, a power of \(+2\) D.)

rows.subtopic: Magnetic Field due to a Current-carrying Conductor
rows.stem:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram to show the pattern of magnetic field lines on a horizontal white board due to a straight current carrying conductor passing perpendicular through its centre. If the direction of current in the conductor is vertically downwards, mark the direction of (i) current, and (ii) magnetic field lines.

(b) State the right hand thumb rule and check whether the directions marked on the diagram are in accordance with this rule.
rows.solution:
(a) Draw a horizontal board with the straight wire passing vertically through its centre. The field lines are concentric circles on the board, centred on the wire, drawn closer together near the wire.

(i) Mark the current with an arrow on the wire pointing vertically downwards.

(ii) Mark the field lines with arrows going clockwise, as seen from above the board.

(b) Right-hand thumb rule: imagine holding the current-carrying straight conductor in your right hand with the thumb pointing in the direction of the current. Then your fingers wrap around the conductor in the direction of the magnetic field lines.

Check: with the thumb pointing downwards along the current, the fingers curl clockwise when seen from above. This is the direction marked on the diagram, so the diagram agrees with the rule.
